newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Insurance innovation key to Singapore windfall.
newsitem.headline: Insurance innovation key to Singapore windfall.

text.p: Singapore's life insurers must innovate to beat other financial firms in the battle for an estimated Singapore $2.0 billion windfall from the Central Provident Fund (CPF), industry chiefs said on Thursday.

"We may have some disadvantage compared to a bank or a fund manager," Tan Beng Lee, chief executive of Great Eastern Life, told Reuters. "We have to overcome it. Perhaps we have to change the way we operate," he said.

Tan said changes were likely to see a move away from the traditional agency sales force towards direct marketing, telesales and even automated transactions through smartcard technology as insurers attempted to get closer to customers.

Insurers predict that S$2.0 billion (US$1.4 billion) could be sunk into insurance and investments over the next three years following the second stage of a three-part liberalisation of Singapore's CPF scheme investment rules.
About S$1.0 billion of CPF funds have been invested in insurance instruments since the first reforms of the compulsory savings scheme in 1993.
The latest, which came into effect on January 1, lowered the minimum qualifying level above which investors can put money into approved investments.
"Part of the gold rush here has been fuelled by CPF since 1993, but we (the industry) certainly can't expect to grow like we did in the past," Tan said.

Insurers in Singapore have grown at annual rates of 20 to 25 percent in the 1990s, but Tan said a more moderate 10 percent was likely in the future, as banks and fund managers rush out products to capitalise on the huge CPF potential.
Tan said the market's biggest players would have to invest in new technology and distribution methods to maintain their positions.

Insurers also have rolled out new products to tempt investors. In the first seven days of 1997, four new schemes were launched by three of the biggest life players in Singapore and more are likely from others.
But Tan Suee Chieh, chief executive of the Singapore arm of Britain's Prudential Assurance, told Reuters that winning the battle would not be easy.

"One has to recognise that there is a need for customer service, but beyond that I see a need for product flexibility and innovation, for good performance, for better training of agents and improvements in the distribution system," he said.

Prudential had significant success in attracting CPF funds released in the 1993 first stage reform, with industry sources estimating the firm's share at 30 percent to 35 percent of the current S$1 billion of CPF funds under management.
Tan Suee Chieh said he believed the type of investor coming to the market after the second stage reform would be more risk averse than the first stage players of 1993.
He said this would be a reason for the success of long term insurance investments over other vehicles.
